I've been working this land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father farmed it before me. I know what this soil wants, and I know what the market needs. There's no reason to change what works.

My land is about 8 mu total. I will plant winter wheat in the autumn, and when I harvest it in June, I will turn around and plant summer maize on the same plots. That's what everyone here does. That's what makes sense on the North China Plain.

For wheat, I'll go to the seed station and get the improved variety the county extension office is pushing this year — probably Jimai or something similar. I'm not going to gamble on some new variety I don't know. I'll rotary till after the maize comes off to chop the stalks under, then sow the wheat. I'll apply the fertilizer all at once at sowing — that's how I've always done it. I'll irrigate three times: once to get germination going if the soil is dry, once at jointing, once at heading. That's what my wheat needs here.

For maize, I'll direct seed right after wheat harvest. No time to lose in June. I'll use a hybrid — Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu, whatever the co-op has. I won't deep till; the soil is fine. Summer rains usually help, but I'll irrigate once if it's dry during the grain-filling period. I put on more nitrogen than some — I'd rather have a big harvest than scrimp and lose yield.

I'll spray pesticide a couple times for each crop. Aphids on the wheat, armyworm on the maize — you have to stay on top of it.
